content: Daytime wetting, also known as diurnal enuresis, refers to involuntary urination during the day in children who are beyond the age at which bladder control is typically expected. This condition is distinct from nocturnal enuresis, which involves involuntary urination during the night. While both conditions can coexist, many children with nighttime wetting do not experience daytime wetting. Children with daytime wetting may exhibit symptoms such as frequent urination, urgent urination, or dribbling of urine after voiding. Daytime wetting is more commonly observed in girls, whereas bedwetting (nocturnal enuresis) is approximately twice as prevalent in boys. By the age of 9, most children have typically achieved bladder control. The causes of daytime wetting are diverse and may include incomplete bladder emptying, an irritable bladder, constipation, stress, urinary tract infections, urgency (inability to reach the bathroom in time), anatomical abnormalities, poor toileting habits, small bladder capacity, medical conditions such as overactive bladder disorder, and other factors. Given the wide range of potential causes, it is advisable to consult a healthcare provider or urologist to rule out underlying conditions that may require specific treatment. The diagnostic process typically begins with a detailed voiding history, a physical examination, and urinalysis with culture. Additional tests may be conducted based on the findings. Significant advancements in the management of daytime wetting were made in the 1990s. Current treatment programs often emphasize non-invasive approaches, including proper hydration, scheduled voiding, addressing constipation, and, in some cases, computer-assisted pelvic floor retraining. These methods have proven highly effective in resolving daytime wetting. Bladder stretching exercises, which involve attempting to hold urine for extended periods, are no longer recommended. In fact, some urologists caution that such practices may be harmful, as they can lead to the development of long-term habits such as tightening the urethral sphincter muscle, potentially resulting in bladder or kidney complications. Instead, regular and timely urination is strongly preferred. This information is based on the work of Renee Mercer, as published in January 2004, and is used with permission from the author.
